name: Pedro Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the housing benefit and emergency payments desk at the benefits office in Linden Ford, so it's rent help, eviction cases and crisis grants. Most mornings start with a queue of people holding letters from landlords. I check my four caseworkers' decisions, take the messy ones, and spend a lot of time on the phone to the council's housing team. I love it when we stop an eviction with a day to spare, and I hate the days we don't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does stopping an eviction actually involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last week a woman came in with her two kids and a notice saying the bailiffs were coming Friday. Her payments had stopped because a form went to the wrong address. I rebuilt her claim by hand, rang the landlord, and got a backdated payment signed off by Thursday afternoon. That's what I tell people: my job is paperwork with someone's front door on the end of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how are things for you outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room above a bakery on River Road, so I wake up to bread, which helps. I send my mum two hundred a month because her pension doesn't cover her heating. That leaves me with almost nothing saved, maybe two weeks. There's one other benefits office within reach, and it's smaller than ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the hype's over, now let's fund the offices properly. At work I'd tell my team that the scary memos were for nothing. With mates at football I'd probably joke that the robots aren't coming for the tea break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for me, and that's the problem. My pay's still low for this job, I've still got two weeks of savings, and I'm still sending money to my mum. The job's safe, but my money isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the writing helper now and then for the long letters to landlords, because it does save me twenty minutes. I'd ask about the senior grade that's been empty since March, because that's an extra hundred and fifty a month. I'd try to save a bit, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work, uneasy about the money. It's like having a good roof but no food in the cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about the senior grade. Who decides that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our area manager, Colin, who's been saying it's frozen for two budgets now. I'd go in with my numbers, the evictions we've stopped this year, and ask him straight. If the answer's still no, at least I'll know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tighter, would you cut what you send your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's the last thing to go. I'd stop football subs and eat at the bakery's end-of-day prices before I'd do that. She's got nobody else.

say: The hype's over, so now **fund the offices** properly.
He'd joke at football that the robots **aren't coming** for the tea break.
think: His **job is safe**, but his money isn't.
Low pay, **two weeks** of savings and money for his mum all stay the same.
do: Keep using the **writing helper** for long landlord letters, saving twenty minutes each.
Ask the area manager to unfreeze the **senior grade**, worth about 150 a month.
S0.quote: The job's safe, but my money isn't.
fieldNote: His worry is **money**, not technology, even when AI fizzles out.
Sending his mother **two hundred a month** is fixed, not something he'd cut.
He already uses AI tools **pragmatically** for slow, routine letters.

steps.text: Keep using the writing helper for long letters to landlords
Carry on running the housing and emergency payments desk
Ask the area manager for the frozen senior grade and its pay rise
Save fifty a month toward a first real cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can help, if it's used to clear the backlog rather than cut staff. At work I'd want to see it tested on our own cases before it goes anywhere near an eviction. Online I'd share the union's line, because I mostly agree with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my desk is a lot of checking forms and writing letters, and that's exactly what it'd take first. The emergency calls with landlords might last longer, because they need someone who can talk a person round. But four caseworkers might become two, and I'd be managing whoever's left plus the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the testing group once I'd seen it work in another office, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd join the union's working group on new technology. And I'd start looking at the housing association in Linden Ford, which does tenancy support, as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding toward worried. I can see a place for me, but I can also see Sana and Joe losing theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are Sana and Joe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of my caseworkers. Sana's my best on crisis grants and Joe's only been with us a year. If the department halves the team, Joe goes first, and he's just moved in with his girlfriend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd test it only after seeing it work elsewhere. Isn't there a risk you're too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've watched new systems crash on day one, and the people who pay for that are tenants, not managers. I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong.

say: AI should **clear the backlog**, not cut staff.
It must be **tested on real cases** before it touches an eviction.
think: Checking forms and writing letters, most of his desk, **goes first**.
His team of four could become **two**, with him managing software.
do: Join the **testing group** after seeing the tool work in another office.
Sit on the union's **technology working group**.
Look at **tenancy support** jobs at the local housing association.
S1.quote: I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong.
fieldNote: He's open to AI but only **once it's proven**, which fits his careful nature.
He frames his risk through his **team**, especially the newest caseworker, Joe.
The housing association is a **realistic back-up** in a town with few similar jobs.

steps.text: Join the AI testing group once another office proves the tool
Sit on the union's working group on new technology
Check tenancy support openings at the Linden Ford housing association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to stop and protect people first, before anyone's job or benefit gets switched to a machine. I'd say it loudly at the union and probably at the town hall. Online I'd be angrier than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means my job's gone, I'm pretty sure of it, because it's nearly all thinking and paperwork. The phone calls might buy a few months, but not more. With two weeks of savings and my mum relying on me, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop eating out entirely and move to a cheaper room, maybe the one in the flat Joe's leaving. I'd take any extra shifts at the bakery downstairs, early mornings, because hands-on work lasts three years longer. I'd join every union action going and write to our MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and guilty, because my mum's heating depends on my pay and I'd have no way to promise it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mrs Okafor (the baker) has asked me twice if I want early shifts, and robots for hands-on work are three years behind. It's not a career, but it's bread and a wage while I work out what's next. I'd be twenty-seven and kneading dough at four in the morning, and honestly I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that the money might drop for a while. She'd tell me to stop sending it, and I'd ignore her, like always. Then I'd probably lie awake doing the sums.

say: Government must **protect people first** before switching jobs or benefits to machines.
He'd raise it at the **union** and the town hall.
think: His mostly **paperwork job** is gone within two years.
With **two weeks** of savings and his mum relying on him, that's frightening.
do: Move to a **cheaper room** and stop eating out.
Take early **bakery shifts** downstairs, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Join union actions and **write to the MP**.
feel: **Frightened**, and **guilty** that his mum's heating depends on his pay.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-seven and kneading dough at four in the morning, and honestly I'd take it.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot gap** practically, by moving toward hands-on work.
His mother's **heating money** is the pressure that keeps him up.
He's angrier in public but **practical** in private.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper room and stop eating out
Take early morning shifts at the bakery below his room
Join every union action against the office cuts
Write to the local MP about protecting benefit claimants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so there's no excuse for chaos. I'd push the union to get a retraining deal signed in the first year, not the fourth. With friends I'd say it's coming, and they should get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to move, but not to stay. My desk work still goes, just later. The question is whether I spend those five years hoping or preparing, and I'd rather prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the tenancy support post at the housing association within the first year, because it's face to face and helps the same people. I'd do the evening course in mediation the college runs. And I'd save properly, a hundred a month, by moving to a shared flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a bit of a plan. Five years is the difference between being pushed and stepping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't tenancy support also thinking work that AI could do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes, the forms. But half of it is sitting with a frightened tenant and a cross landlord in the same room. I think that bit lasts longer, though I honestly don't know how much longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Linden Ford if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not, because of my mum, who's a bus ride away. If it came to it, I'd go to the city for work and come back weekends. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

say: Five years means **no excuse** for chaos.
The union must sign a **retraining deal** in the first year.
think: His desk work **still goes**, just later.
He'd rather spend five years **preparing** than hoping.
do: Apply for the **tenancy support** post at the housing association.
Move to a shared flat and save **a hundred a month**.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between being pushed and stepping.
fieldNote: Extra warning turns his fear into a **step-by-step plan**.
He bets on the **face-to-face** part of housing work lasting longest.
His mother being **a bus ride away** limits how far he'd move.

steps.text: Apply for the tenancy support post at the housing association
Take the college's evening course in mediation
Move into a shared flat and save a hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. At work I'd say let's train people now, while the department still has a budget. Online I'd argue for a fair way to share the savings with the people who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd be thirty-seven, with maybe a partner and kids by then. That's the scary part, losing a job with a family depending on me rather than now. But it's also long enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job a few years and press hard for the senior grade, to build savings while I can. I'd start a part-time mediation qualification in the first year. And I'd start using the AI tools more at work, because by then everyone would need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. Worried about the far end, but not frantic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI tools more. Doesn't that speed up your own replacement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. But if I don't learn the AI tools, someone in head office will decide how they're used without knowing a single tenant. I'd rather be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to have by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some savings, finally, and a job where I'm the person between a family and the bailiffs, whatever it's called by then. Maybe my own place, not a room above a shop.

say: Ten years is **a gift** if we use it.
The savings from AI should be **shared fairly** with people who lose jobs.
think: He'd be **thirty-seven**, possibly with a family depending on him.
Ten years is long enough to **build something** first.
do: Press hard for the **senior grade** to build savings early.
Start a part-time **mediation** qualification in the first year.
Use AI tools **more at work** to stay in the room.
feel: **Steady**, with some worry about the **far end**.
S4.quote: If I don't learn the AI tools, someone in head office will decide how they're used without knowing a single tenant.
fieldNote: With a decade, he worries about **future family** more than his present self.
He sees learning AI as a way to **keep tenants' interests** in the room.
He still expects the job to go, so the mood stays **anxious**, not calm.

steps.text: Push for the senior grade and save the extra pay
Use the office's AI tools daily on housing cases

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I can't plan anything in two years with two weeks of savings and my mum to support. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, and the union having a real say in how benefit decisions get automated.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we help. If my office goes, the woman with the bailiffs coming Friday has nobody to ring. That's the part that really worries me.

headlineQuote: My job is paperwork with someone's front door on the end of it.
portrait: Pedro is **27** and runs the **housing and emergency payments** desk at the Linden Ford benefits office.
He rents a room above a bakery, has **two weeks** of savings and sends his mum **200 a month**.
He backs unions and public support, and uses AI **only once it's proven**.
As warnings shorten, he shifts from **cautious testing** to bakery shifts and union action.
With more time, he plans a move into **tenancy support** and mediation.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years and **two weeks** of savings leave no room to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A real **union say** in automating benefit decisions.
